stem: Elements of group 16 generally show lower values of first ionisation enthalpy compared to the elements of corresponding period of group 15. Why ?
solution: Group 15 elements have extra stable, half filled p-orbitals with electronic configuration \(\mathrm{(ns^2np^3)}\). Therefore more amount of energy is required to remove an electron compared to that of the partially filled orbitals \(\mathrm{(ns^2np^4)}\) of group 16 elements of the corresponding period.

stem: The values of first ionisation enthalpy of S and Cl are 1000 and 1256 kJ mol\(^{-1}\), respectively. Explain the observed trend.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the printed solution says S and Cl "belong to second period of the periodic table". They belong to the THIRD period — Table 7.1 of this same chapter gives their configurations as \(\mathrm{[Ne]3s^23p^4}\) and \(\mathrm{[Ne]3s^23p^5}\). The argument and the conclusion S < Cl are unaffected, so the solution is preserved as printed.]

The elements S and Cl belong to second period of the periodic table.

Across a period effective nuclear charge increases and atomic size decreases with increase in atomic number.

Therefore the energy required for the removal of electron from the valence shell (I.E.) increases in the order S < Cl.

stem: Why is there a large difference between the melting and boiling points of oxygen and sulfur ?
solution:
Oxygen exists as diatomic molecule \(\mathrm{(O_2)}\) where as sulfur exists as polyatomic molecule \(\mathrm{(S_8)}\).

The van der Waals forces of attraction between \(\mathrm{O_2}\) molecules are relatively weak owing to its much smaller size.

The large van der Waals attractive forces in the \(\mathrm{S_8}\) molecules can be noticed because of large molecular size. Therefore oxygen has low m.p. and b.p. as compared to sulfur.

stem: Fluorine has less negative electron gain affinity than chlorine. Why ?
solution: The size of fluorine atom is smaller than chlorine atom. As a result, there are strong inter electronic repulsions in the relatively small 2p orbitals of fluorine and therefore, the incoming electron does not experience much attraction. Thus fluorine has less negative electron gain affinity than chlorine.

stem: Bond dissociation enthalpy of \(\mathrm{F_2}\) (158.8 kJ mol\(^{-1}\)) is lower than that of \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) (242.6 kJ mol\(^{-1}\)) Why ?
solution: Fluorine has small atomic size than chlorine. The lone pairs on each F atoms in \(\mathrm{F_2}\) molecule are so close together that they strongly repel each other, and make the F - F bond weak (fig. 7.1) Thus it requires less amount of energy to break the F - F bond. In \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) molecule the lone pairs on each Cl atom are at a larger distance and the repulsion is negligible. Thus Cl - Cl bond is comparatively stronger. Therefore bond dissociation enthalpy of \(\mathrm{F_2}\) is lower than that of \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\).

stem: Noble gases have very low melting and boiling points. Why ?
solution: Noble gases are monoatomic, the only type of inter atomic interactions which exist between them are van der Waals forces. Therefore, they can be liquified at very low temperatures and have very low melting or boiling points.

stem: Which form of sulfur shows paramagnetic behaviour ?
solution: In vapour state, sulfur partly exists as \(\mathrm{S_2}\) molecule, which has two unpaired electrons in the antibonding \(\pi^*\) orbitals like \(\mathrm{O_2}\). Hence it exhibits paramagnetism.

stem: Dioxygen is paramagnetic inspite of having even number of electrons. Explain.
solution:
Dioxygen is a covalently bonded molecule.

\(:\ddot{\mathrm{O}}::\ddot{\mathrm{O}}:\) or \(:\ddot{\mathrm{O}}=\ddot{\mathrm{O}}:\)

Paramagnetic behaviour of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) can be explained with the help of molecular orbital theory.

Electronic configuration of \(\mathrm{O_2}\)

\(\mathrm{KK}\ \sigma(2s)^2\ \sigma^*(2s)^2\ \sigma(2p_z)^2\ \pi(2p_x)^2\ \pi(2p_y)^2\ \pi^*(2p_x)^1\ \pi^*(2p_y)^1\).

Presence of two unpaired electrons explains paramagnetic nature of dioxygen.

stem: High concentration of ozone can be dangerously explosive. Explain.
solution:
i. Thermal stability : Ozone is thermodynamically unstable than oxygen and decomposes into \(\mathrm{O_2}\). The decomposition is exothermic and results in the liberation of heat (\(\Delta H\) is -ve) and an increase in entropy (\(\Delta S\) is positive). This results in large negative Gibbs energy change (\(\Delta G\)). Therefore high concentration of ozone can be dangerously explosive.

Eq. \(\mathrm{O_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{O_2} + \mathrm{O}\)

stem: What is the action of concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) on (a) HBr (b) HI
solution:
Concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises hydrobromic acid to bromine.

\(2\mathrm{HBr} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Br_2} + \mathrm{SO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

It oxidises hydroiodic acid to iodine.

\(2\mathrm{HI} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{I_2} + \mathrm{SO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
